newsitem.title: USA: Jury in Reynolds trial resumes deliberations.
newsitem.headline: Jury in Reynolds trial resumes deliberations.

text.p: Jurors resumed deliberations on Monday in a wrongful death lawsuit against the R.J. Reynolds Tobacco Co. to decide whether the company made a dangerous product and negligently caused the death of a smoker.

The panel, five women and one man, began its second day of discussions shortly before 9 a.m. EDT, and was still deliberating at noon. Court officials said the jurors chose to have lunch sent in so they could continue working.
Jurors deliberated for nearly two hours late Friday after listening to more than five hours of closing arguments from the two sides.
Plaintiff Dana Raulerson alleged that Reynolds' negligence caused the death of her sister, Jean Connor, a heavy smoker who died of lung cancer in 1995 at age 49.

Connor developed a three-pack-a-day habit before she was diagnosed with lung cancer in 1993. She filed a product liability lawsuit against Reynolds before her death. Raulerson took up the case as a wrongful death action when Connor died.
The trial, initially expected to last two or three weeks, entered its fifth week on Monday.

The three-page verdict form given to jurors Friday asks them to answer two key questions: "Was there negligence on the part of Defendant R.J. Reynolds Tobacco Company which was a legal cause of the death of decedent, Jean Connor?" and "Were the cigarettes manufactured by Defendant R.J. Reynolds Tobacco Company unreasonably dangerous and defective and a legal cause of the death of decedent, Jean Connor?"

If the jurors answer "yes" to those two questions, they will be asked to decide whether Connor filed her lawsuit too late. Under Florida law, plaintiffs have four years to file a lawsuit from the time they were aware of their injury.

If the panel decides the lawsuit was filed on time, it will be asked to determine the loss to Connor's estate from her death at 49; her medical and funeral expenses, the value of the pain and suffering of her three children and any punitive damages they want to assess against the company.

In another case involving the tobacco industry, a state judge in Miami cautioned attorneys for both sides about publicly discussing the upcoming trial of a class-action lawsuit against cigarette makers and said he would consider an industry request for a gag order.
"I don't want a prejudiced jury," said Dade County Circuit Judge Robert Kaye. "... If you really want a fair jury, you are going to have to be circumspect in the things you say and do."

Philip Morris Cos. Inc. on Friday asked the court to impose a gag order on Stanley Rosenblatt, who represents thousands of flight attendants in the lawsuit against the tobacco industry alleging secondhand cigarette smoke made them sick.
The trial, the first ever of a class-action lawsuit against cigarette makers, is due to begin June 2.
Philip Morris attorney David Hardy said Rosenblatt acted improperly by leaking to The Miami Herald the transcript of videotaped depositions taken from tobacco industry chief executive officers.
Rosenblatt also showed excerpts from those depositions on the CBS television show 60 Minutes on Sunday night.

Rosenblatt contended that media interest in the tobacco industry was extremely intense, having nothing to do with his involvement. "The concept of drumming up publicity on this case is absurd on its face," he said.
Attorneys for The Wall Street Journal, Miami Herald and USA Today asked the court not to impose a gag order.
